newsitem.title: JAPAN: MOF says not yet directed to draw up extra budget.
newsitem.headline: MOF says not yet directed to draw up extra budget.

text.p: Japan's Ministry of Finance (MOF) has not yet been directed by its minister to start preparing a supplementary budget for this fiscal year, Vice Finance Minister Tadashi Ogawa told a news conference on Monday.

Asked whether Finance Minister Wataru Kubo had directed his ministry to start preparations for a supplementary budget which includes economic stimulus measures after talking with Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, Ogawa said: "We have not received any instructions."

A ruling coaltion party official said earlier that Hashimoto and Kubo agreed on Sunday that the government should decide whether to draft an extra budget for 1996/97 to stimulate the economy after seeing GDP data for the April to June period. They also agreed that a final decision on the extra budget should be made sometime after September 20.
Ogawa reiterated his view that now was not the time to start considering a supplementary budget as the economy was slowly, but surely, heading towards recovery.
"What we must do now is to implement steadily the original 1996/97 budget," he said.

Asked about the schedule for resuming talks with the United States on a dispute over a bilateral insurance pact, Ogawa said nothing had been decided yet and Japan had not taken an initiative in starting the talks.
"But I hope the talks will start soon," he said.
After bilateral negotiations broke off last month, the two countries agreed to resume again after September 2.

Asked about the possibility of issuing deficit-financing bonds to fill an estimated gap of 21 trillion yen between revenue and spending expected in next fiscal year's budget, Ogawa said worsening conditions in state finances must be taken seriously into account when finalising next year's budget.

On the huge debt accumulated by the former national railway which has been privatised into seven Japan Railway companies, Ogawa said that although the remaining debt would have to be shouldered by the public in the end, he hoped to work with other ministries to minimise the burden.
